title: Segment Tree: Range Minimum Query with Updates
oneLiner: Design a RangeMinTree with update(index, val) and queryMin(left, right), both O(log n): the case a Fenwick tree can't handle.
keyTakeaway: A segment tree works for any associative combine, not just +: swap the sum for Math.Min and the identity 0 for int.MaxValue (infinity), and the same build, update and query give range minimums. A Fenwick tree can't, because its range query is prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1), and there is no way to "subtract out" a minimum.
explanation:
Build a class RangeMinTree over an int array with update(index, val), which sets nums[index] = val, and queryMin(left, right), which returns the smallest of nums[left..right], inclusive. Range minimum query, or RMQ, shows up directly (lowest price in a time window, closest free slot) and inside other algorithms (lowest common ancestor via an Euler tour, longest common prefix of suffixes).

The segment tree from Range Sum Query, Mutable works unchanged once you swap two things. The combine becomes min(left, right) instead of left + right. The value returned for a node completely outside the query becomes the identity for min, the value that never wins: int.MaxValue in C#, float('inf') or a large sentinel in Python. Each node then stores the minimum of its range, an update recomputes the log n ancestors of a leaf with min, and a query takes the min of the nodes that lie completely inside [left, right].

Why it works: min is associative, meaning min(min(a, b), c) = min(a, min(b, c)). The tree groups elements in its own fixed way, and associativity says the grouping can't change the answer. So the same code works for max, gcd, bitwise AND / OR / XOR, or a product modulo m.

Why a Fenwick tree doesn't: a Fenwick tree only answers prefixes, and gets a range as prefix(r) minus prefix(l - 1). That needs an inverse operation. Knowing min(nums[0..r]) = 1 and min(nums[0..l - 1]) = 1 tells you nothing about min(nums[l..r]).

If the array never changed, a sparse table would answer each query in O(1) after an O(n log n) build (it precomputes the minimum of every window whose length is a power of two, and covers [l, r] with two overlapping windows). Updates break it, which is why this problem wants a segment tree.

The harness builds new RangeMinTree(nums), then runs each operation in order: "update" with [index, val] and "queryMin" with [left, right], and returns the queryMin results. One test has int.MaxValue in the array, so a sentinel must not collide with real data in a way that breaks the answer.

Done. Same shape and same O(log n) costs as the sum tree; only the combine (min) and the identity (+infinity) changed.

recognitionSignals: Minimum or maximum over a sliding or arbitrary range, with point updates in between.
Any associative "combine" (min, max, gcd, AND, OR) over ranges that change: a segment tree, not a Fenwick tree.
The array is static and only queried: a sparse table gives O(1) queries instead.
gotchas: The outside-the-range value must be the identity for min (int.MaxValue or infinity), not 0, or every range containing a positive minimum returns 0.
Don't add to the leaf: update replaces the value, then recomputes each ancestor as the min of its two children.
Allocate 4n slots, and handle a 1-element array (the root is the leaf).
confusableWith: Segment Tree: Range Sum Query, Mutable (this track) is the same structure with + and identity 0.
Monotonic Deque: Sliding Window Maximum (Patterns) also needs range extremes, but only for windows that slide one step at a time, so a monotonic deque does it in O(n) total.

complexity.note: Per operation, the same as the sum tree: one root-to-leaf path for an update, O(log n) nodes for a query, and an O(n) build. The 4n-slot array is O(n) space.
